rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-2: many owners of eligible cars value the rebate above their car and the cost of buying sooner (1.1 million eligible cars against V$4,000).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-1: sellers do not capture the whole rebate; some 30 competing brands; the rebate is shown on the invoice.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-2 with SB-2's premise: buyers who take the rebate buy a new car they would not have bought in the window.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-7: the supply of eligible models cannot grow much within six months (shipping lead times of three to five months).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-16: while their stock is fixed by earlier import orders, sellers have clearly fewer alternatives than rebate buyers, who can wait or keep their car.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-12: some rebate buyers would otherwise have bought a non-eligible new model.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-8: some owners of failing cars can get a roadworthiness certificate for less than the rebate is worth to them.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-9: importers and dealers have an existing association.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-6: demand for rebates exceeds 120,000 at some point in the window (1.1 million eligible cars).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-5: buyers knew of the scheme from March and could delay purchases.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-3: many window buyers would have bought a new car within the next few years anyway.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-4: the scrapped cars would otherwise have stayed in use (roadworthiness required; retirement at about 18 years).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-13: used-car imports cannot quickly replace the scrapped cars (25% duty and inspection).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-20: buyers do not expect a repeat scheme (the opposite of A-15, p = 0.35); ministers have said there is no plan to repeat it.

No matching assumption in WE-019; judged from the text: new cars are imported against volumes ordered months ahead (shipping lead times), so at the end of the window import volumes set for the boom cannot be cut at once; WE-019 signs the post-window price fall (C-25) and calls it weak.
